decisions.question: e-9492

source.question: e-9492
source.value:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=1-\sin{\theta},$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = -\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, the expression for our line integral is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2-2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

source.value:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
\int_C \,\textrm d s = L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\textrm d s$ is given by

$$
\textrm ds = \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r = r(\theta)$ for $\theta_1 \leq \theta \leq \theta_2,$ we have

$$
L=	\int_C \,\textrm d s =  \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} \sqrt{r^2 +\left(\frac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta}\right)^2 }\,\textrm{d}\theta.
$$

Since $r=2(1+\sin\theta),$ we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}r}{\textrm{d}\theta} = 2\cos{\theta}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{4(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2}+4{(\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{2+2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta \end{aligned}
$$

Next, we recall the following identities:

$$
\begin{aligned}{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})=1,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\end{aligned}
$$

Rewriting our integral using the above identities, we can evaluate it as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}L & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+{cos}^{2}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }\sqrt{{(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2}))}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}{\int }_{0}^{\pi }|\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})|\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{2}{[-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\theta }{2})]}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =4\sqrt{2}(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2}))-(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)) \\  & =4\sqrt{2}((0+1)-(-1+0)) \\  & =8\sqrt{2}\end{aligned}
$$
